text: This chapter has covered three real controls on their own — secrets scanning, least privilege for pipeline identities, and software bills of materials. This last lesson pulls them into one thing: a concrete checklist a change has to pass before it reaches production, and more importantly, a way to make that checklist actually enforced instead of a document people forget to open.

The first half of the gate comes straight from this chapter. One: the secrets scan is clean, on this diff and against an already baseline-audited history. Two: no long-lived static credential got introduced — new cloud access uses OIDC federation or a short-lived token. Three: CI and CD permissions are explicit and minimal, no job holding a broader role than the resource it actually touches. Four: untrusted and trusted execution stay separated, so a fork-triggered job never has a path to production secrets.

The second half closes it out. Five: an SBOM was generated for this build and scanned, with no unresolved critical or high findings left unreviewed. Six: dependencies and base images are pinned to exact versions, not a floating latest tag, so what ships is reproducible later. Seven: branch protection and required reviews are enforced on the target branch. Eight: the deploy itself is logged and attributable — who approved it, which commit SHA shipped, and where that build's reports live.

Writing all eight down somewhere doesn't make them happen. Expressing them as actual CI jobs does — a secrets-scan job running gitleaks, and an sbom-and-scan job that generates an SBOM with syft and fails the build on any high-severity finding from grype. Both run automatically on every pull request, with no step depending on a person remembering to run them by hand.

The piece that makes those jobs binding, not just informational, is branch protection. Mark secrets-scan and sbom-and-scan as required status checks on the target branch, alongside requiring at least one approving review. With that configured, the merge button itself won't go green until every item on the checklist has actually passed — the gate becomes structural, not something anyone has to remember.

That closes out securing the pipeline itself: credentials never sit exposed in a commit, every identity running the pipeline is scoped and short-lived, every dependency going into a build is inventoried and checked, and none of it reaches production without that gate passing first.
